clue.text: Argue over something that Jack Sprat would never do

definitions.meaning: the idiom for talking a matter over at length, often argumentatively

definitions.text: something that Jack Sprat would never do
definitions.meaning: in the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so he would never literally chew it

explanation.surface: A quarrel over the one thing the fussy nursery-rhyme man refuses to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is read literally: Jack Sprat, of the rhyme 'Jack Sprat could eat no fat', would never put fat in his mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to talk or dispute something at length, so it matches debating a point.

clue.text: Farquhar is sampling somewhat spicy paste

indicators.note: somewhat means only a part, so just a stretch of the preceding words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the name, the whole of the next word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A man called Farquhar tries a little of a hot condiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sampling' looks like the signal for a hidden word, but it is part of the fodder: the answer ends in its first two letters, and 'somewhat' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Harissa is a North African chilli paste, a hot relish used in cooking and at the table.

clue.text: Turn left following a thrilling exclamation

indicators.note: in this down entry, one piece following another means it is placed after it

parts.note: the cry of delight on a fairground ride
the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A driver swings to the left after a joyful shout.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is read backwards to the order of the answer: the letter for 'left' comes after the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheel is to pivot or swing round, as troops or birds do, a verb synonym for rotating.

clue.text: Good-looking husband? Not half!

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for husband
'and some!' is a British exclamation of emphatic agreement, like 'not half!'

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the husband is attractive and gets an enthusiastic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', and so is 'and some!'; it looks like an instruction to halve something but is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Handsome describes an attractive person, especially a man, so it is a straight adjective synonym.

clue.text: Revise, refer, check Mann's 1941 novel

indicators.note: to revise text is to rework it, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: all fifteen letters of the three words are used

explanation.surface: An editor is told to check a reference to a Thomas Mann book from 1941.
explanation.walkthrough: Mann's name points to Thomas Mann, but he is only fodder: the novel is by Daphne du Maurier, a romance set in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphne du Maurier published this historical romance about a pirate in 1941, so it is the book described.

clue.text: Lightly touch punctilious person having removed clothes

indicators.note: clothes are the outer layer, so the punctilious person loses the letters at each end

parts.note: a stickler insists on exact correctness

explanation.surface: A fussy person undresses and is gently touched.
explanation.walkthrough: The clothes are the first and last letters, which are stripped away to leave the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To tickle is to stroke skin gently with the fingers, so a light caress is the verb sense.

clue.text: Old northerner selected for the team, according to the radio

indicators.note: on the radio words are heard, not seen, so the answer is spelt as something that is only spoken

parts.note: a player chosen for a side has been picked

explanation.surface: A radio sports report says an old Scot has been chosen for the side.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were an ancient people of northern Scotland, hence an old northerner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Picts lived in what is now northern and eastern Scotland in late Roman and early medieval times.

clue.text: Explosive Colditz inmate placed above the German Kommandant's head say?

definitions.note: adjective in the clue; the answer is a noun for a volatile situation

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece placed above another comes first in the answer

parts.note: Colditz was a German castle holding Allied prisoners of war
German for 'the' in the masculine

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the Kommandant is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the camp commander's title
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say, an apple'

explanation.surface: A wartime prisoner plots something explosive over the camp commander's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The Colditz setting pulls toward escape stories, but it only supplies a prisoner of war; 'say' gives the abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation likely to erupt into violence is called this, from the barrel that once stored gunpowder.

clue.text: Furnishing lorry almost overturned on the road to Edinburgh

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece on another sits above it, so the lorry comes before the road
a vehicle overturned is upside down, and in a down entry the shortened lorry is read upwards
almost means not quite complete, so the lorry loses its last letter

parts.note: a truck is a lorry
the A1 is the trunk road from London to Edinburgh, with 1 read as I, and N for the northward direction signed as A1 (N)

explanation.surface: A furniture lorry nearly overturns on the great road north to Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: Shorten the lorry, turn it round, and follow it with the A1 heading north; the digit 1 stands for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Curtains are soft furnishings, the fabric hangings that dress a window in a home.

clue.text: Scottish bank daring? Not very

indicators.note: 'not very' asks for the daring word without the letter standing for very

parts.note: brave means daring
the standard abbreviation for very, which is taken away

explanation.surface: A Scottish bank asks whether it is bold and answers 'not very'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests money, but here it is a slope; brae is the Scots word for a hillside or riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots a brae is a steep slope or hillside, especially one beside a river.

clue.text: Christmas jersey commercial featuring Romeo, a witty Englishman

a Jersey is a breed of dairy cow
an advertisement
R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.definitionFit: The playwright and songwriter of Private Lives was celebrated as the wittiest Englishman of his era.

clue.text: Starts to play Sting's charity songs

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, taken from the next two words

parts.note: the opening letter of each word
alms are gifts to the poor

explanation.surface: A band begins performing the singer Sting's songs for a good cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting reads as the pop star, but only his initial is wanted; the songs are sacred ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalms are the sacred hymns of the Book of Psalms, sung in church worship.

clue.text: Accused criminal accepting trial ultimately is a dead end

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the accused word takes in the letter from the trial
criminal means crooked, so the letters of the accused, with the extra one taken in, are bent into a new order

parts.note: the word itself is the fodder

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of the trial is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A defendant who agrees to go to trial finds it leads nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter from 'trial' joins the fodder before it is rearranged, so eight letters are mixed, not seven.
explanation.definitionFit: A cul-de-sac is a street closed at one end, from French for 'bottom of the bag'.

clue.text: American mother chasing a comical chap? That's quite seedy

indicators.note: one thing chasing another runs behind it, so the mother goes after the comical chap

parts.note: a card is a funny, eccentric person
the article as written, the second one in the clue
the American spelling of mum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seedy' suggests something sordid, but the definition is literal: the spice is sold as seed pods.
explanation.definitionFit: The spice is made from the aromatic seeds of a ginger-family plant, so it is full of seeds.

clue.text: Senior detective's upset Met over a whitewash

parts.note: DI is a detective inspector, with the possessive S

indicators.note: upset means turned over, and in a down entry the Met is read from the bottom up

parts.note: the Metropolitan Police of London
as in 'ten pounds a head', meaning each

explanation.walkthrough: 'Whitewash' looks like a cover-up but is the paint itself; 'a' means per, as in a price per item.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is a cheap water-based paint used on walls and ceilings, like limewash or whitewash.

clue.text: Philosopher, king, soldier

parts.note: K for king, as in chess notation
a soldier ant is a kind of ant

explanation.walkthrough: The soldier is an insect: soldier ants are the fighting caste of a colony.
explanation.definitionFit: Immanuel Kant was the German Enlightenment thinker who wrote the Critique of Pure Reason.

clue.text: Still bored by Mary, terribly ordinary person

indicators.note: to be bored by something is to have a hole drilled through you, so the still word has the name set inside it

parts.note: as in 'even more', meaning still more

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly, so the name's letters come out jumbled

parts.note: the name itself is the fodder

explanation.surface: Mary is so boring that everyone around her stays motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is an adverb meaning even, not calm; the jumbled name goes in after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman is the typical common person, after the medieval morality play whose hero represents all humanity.

clue.text: Absence of American intelligence?

parts.note: no means none, a lack
the United States

explanation.surface: A sneer that Americans are short of brains.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a jibe at Americans; read in pieces it is simply 'no' plus the country's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is a British informal word for common sense or practical wit, from Greek for mind.

clue.text: Partly extend across completed Grand Prix circuit

parts.note: a finished thing is over
one circuit of a racetrack

explanation.surface: A racing driver finishes a lap of the Grand Prix track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circuit' looks like the whole track, but it is a single time round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that overlap cover part of one another, like roof tiles lying across each other's edges.

clue.text: Drive a vintage Rolls

parts.note: both words, eight letters in all

explanation.surface: Take an old Rolls-Royce out for a spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like the car, Rolls-Royce, but it is a verb telling you to tumble the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To navigate is to steer a course, so directing a vehicle along a route matches.

clue.text: Trade vehicles in transit

definitions.meaning: dealing, often illicit, as in drug trafficking
cars and lorries moving on the roads

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both commercial dealing in goods and the stream of cars on the road.

clue.text: Order child to turn over shabby clothes

explanation.definitionFit: A diktat is a decree imposed without consultation, a German loanword for a harsh command.

clue.text: Stew of rice, ale and cold vegetable

C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.definitionFit: Celeriac is a celery variety grown for its knobbly edible root.

clue.text: Members of group regularly yawn, lying around part of airport

the article as written
the standard abbreviation for wife

clue.text: Shocked Spooner reports assault on painter Francis
